The station garden had survived three years without a regular train. Mint grew between the platform stones, and a young tree had taken root beside the signal box. Mara brought a broom from the waiting room. The timetable behind the glass still promised a morning departure, although the hands had been removed from the platform clock before the roof was repaired.

“Keep the mint along the edge,” Mara said. She drew the broom inward to show where the path should run. Ellis had planted those roots after the last storm, and pulling them out would leave the soil bare. A basket of spare gloves waited on the bench beside a tin of old tickets. Nobody had decided what to do with the tickets yet.

Jonah examined the tree beside the signal box. He pressed the soil with the heel of a boot. “This one needs a wider space,” Jonah replied. The branches reached across the entrance, brushing the glass whenever the wind moved. A circle of lighter dust showed where a sign had once warned visitors to keep clear of the door. The sign itself was missing.

A cart rattled along the lane beyond the station wall. The sound faded before its owner came into view. Mara swept another length of platform while Jonah loosened the earth around the tree. In the waiting room, the unopened windows held the smell of paper and summer heat. The work was slow enough for every change to become visible.

Niko appeared at the far gate with a bucket of water. They paused beside the bench to put on a pair of gloves. “I found the missing sign under the counter,” Niko said. The painted letters had survived, but the wood behind them was soft. Niko placed the bucket beneath the tree and laid the sign flat in the shade, where it could dry without curling.

“We can copy it onto the new board,” Mara replied. She leaned the broom against the wall and measured the old sign with a length of string. Jonah made a shallow channel around the roots. Niko poured the water slowly until the channel filled. For the first time that morning, the station looked ready to receive someone, even if nobody arrived by train.
